analysis.one_liner: Bans sulfide-ore copper mining on federal land upstream of the Boundary Waters wilderness.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Natural Resources Committee upon introduction, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes permanent a federal withdrawal of about 225,504 acres of Superior National Forest in Minnesota's Rainy River Watershed, the waters that flow into the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. It removes those lands from mining claims and mineral leasing, specifically blocking sulfide-ore copper mining, whose acidic runoff threatens the wilderness's water quality. It still allows the Forest Service to permit removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite if that does not harm the watershed's water, air, and forest habitat.
analysis.who_benefits: People who canoe, camp, and fish in the Boundary Waters; the region's tourism and outfitting economy, which the bill's findings say would add 1,500 to 4,600 jobs and $100 million to $900 million in income over 20 years with a mining ban; and the Ojibwe bands whose treaty hunting and fishing rights cover the area.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tourism economy, canoeists, and Ojibwe tribes

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws about 225,504 acres of federal land and water from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and disposal, permanently blocking sulfide-ore copper mining in the watershed upstream of the Boundary Waters.
Protects an amenity and tourism economy the bill's findings say would grow by 1,500 to 4,600 more jobs and $100 million to $900 million more income over 20 years with a mining ban than without one.

Guards the treaty rights of the Grand Portage, Fond du Lac, and Bois Forte Ojibwe bands, who hold hunting and fishing rights across northeast Minnesota and whose communities depend on the health of these waters.

Prevents acid mine drainage, a form of pollution the bill's findings say has affected water quality at copper sulfide mines reviewed in a peer-reviewed study of 14 operating U.S. mines, all of which experienced spills or accidental releases.

analysis.who_pays: Sulfide-ore copper and nickel mining companies lose access to the withdrawn federal minerals, including any project they might have developed in the watershed. The nation forgoes a domestic source of copper and nickel that could have supported battery and electrification supply chains, and the surrounding area forgoes the direct mining jobs such a project would have created.

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal is permanent and project-blind: it bans all sulfide-ore mining in the watershed outright, rather than letting any specific mine proposal face its own environmental review, and it takes privately held mineral rights off the table for national minerals policy.
The United States forgoes potential domestic copper and nickel production in a region where mining jobs pay well, a real cost for some nearby communities even as the tourism economy grows.

The job and income figures favoring protection come from studies cited in the bill's own findings, prepared by the bill's supporters, so they should be weighed as advocacy-backed estimates rather than neutral projections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is real but lopsided. On one side is a permanent, hard-to-reverse pollution risk: acidic mine runoff in a network of roughly 2,000 connected lakes and 1,200 miles of canoe routes, where cleanup of sulfide-ore contamination is famously difficult. On the other is a single mining project's jobs and a marginal addition to national copper and nickel supply. An honest weighing favors protection here, though the bill's blanket approach forecloses even carefully sited proposals, and the pro-tourism job estimates are the work of the bill's allies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went straight to the House Natural Resources Committee when it was introduced in January 2025 and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Betty McCollum introduced the bill on January 21, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
Forty-one House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans did.

The bill would write into law a 2023 Interior Department decision (Public Land Order 7917) that withdrew the same 225,504 acres for 20 years, restoring a protection the Trump administration had canceled in 2018 and reinitiated under President Biden in 2021.

Because the bill has never left committee, it has received no floor vote in either chamber and the 2023 withdrawal it would codify rests on executive action that can be reversed by a later administration rather than on statute.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled, the wilderness protection rests only on an executive order that can be undone, leaving sulfide-ore mining companies better positioned than they would be under a statutory ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the mining industry and its allies

for.name: 41 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans joined.

for.name: Grand Portage, Fond du Lac, and Bois Forte Bands of Ojibwe
for.role: Tribal nations with treaty rights in the region
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed permanent protection of the watershed, which the bill's findings acknowledge through their treaty-based legal interest in the area's resources.

against.name: Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup since its referral in January 2025.

against.name: Sulfide-ore copper mining industry (including Twin Metals Minnesota)
against.role: Mining companies holding claims and leases in the Rainy River Watershed
against.what_they_did: Opposed the withdrawal, including through litigation and lobbying, because the bill would permanently bar copper and nickel mining on lands where they hold mineral rights.

against.name: 223 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, and the Republican majority controls the committee calendar that has kept it from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors are House Democrats, no House Republicans signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican majority that has taken no action on it.

industries.note: The bill permanently removes about 225,504 acres from mining claims and leasing, ending the industry's path to the minerals under the Rainy River Watershed. Its profit depends on extracting sulfide ore in a watershed whose runoff feeds pristine lakes, so its interest runs directly against protecting the wilderness's water.

industries.industry: Wilderness tourism and outfitting (lodges, canoe outfitters, guides)
industries.note: The bill locks in the region's canoe and recreation economy, which the bill's findings say would add 1,500 to 4,600 jobs and $100 million to $900 million in income over 20 years under a mining ban. The industry's growth depends on the same clean water the public wants protected.

industries.industry: Iron ore, taconite, and aggregate producers
industries.note: The bill explicitly allows the Forest Service to permit removal of sand, gravel, granite, iron ore, and taconite from the withdrawn area, provided it does not harm the watershed's water, air, and forest habitat.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority and chairing Natural Resources, and with the Trump administration moving in 2025 to rescind the 2023 mineral withdrawal this bill would codify, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote in this Congress. Its realistic best use is as a marker for future legislation; the underlying protection currently lives or dies by executive action rather than statute.
